doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Beijing trip with Jon Jang
summary: He went to a Beijing jazz festival with Jon Jang, speaks of Asian jazz musicians' authenticity, and of hugs and Tiananmen Square.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I see you’ve even been to Beijing?

I went to Beijing with my friend Jon Jang, which is a perfect example of the openness I found here on the West Coast, like with the Asian Jazz Society and people who are Asians, they’re saying lookit, man, we’ve been playing this music since it began too. There were jazz bands in China in the forties. This isn’t like something that’s foreign to them. We’ve been living with you maniacs all these years so we are authentic jazz musicians. And so Jon is one of these guys.

Jang. J-A-N-G. And he goes between a love for his Chinese music and a love for Duke Ellington and modern jazz music and he plays with people like David Murray and all of these — and so we went to Beijing for some kind of — I don’t know how they got us over there, it was some kind of basic Beijing Jazz Festival, which was only attended by the very rich, like a one time event. There’s a lot of those in different parts of the world, where the aristocrats or the ruling people, they like jazz and they have enough money to import it. And it was a very interesting experience. I really love Beijing, I’ll tell you that. I mean the people there were just wonderful. Boy oh boy. A nation that understands the meaning of a nice hug.

They do. They’ll give you a hug, the young kids and it’s really great. I really enjoyed it over there. And it’s sort of — I went to Tiananmen Square and it was sort of, there was a big tension with the soldiers, because the soldiers there, you know like our soldiers here, at least you can say, “Hey how you doing, buddy?” Their soldiers are really stiff and really rigid and you don’t fool around with them at all. You don’t have conversation. But the people are just very friendly and want to know where you’re from and da-da-da. And maybe like fifty yards away from the center of Tiananmen Square there’s a McDonald’s. The Golden Arches are everywhere. So you’re not totally away from home.
